content.summary_of_the_paper: The current study proposes hierarchical improving heuristics for solving large-scale CVRP. It uses a Clockwise clustering approach to decompose nodes into subgroups and apply improving heuristics to solve the decomposed subproblems. The core part of the current study is to learn a local operator that chooses the edges for k-opt moves. The present study structures the edge selection policy using encoder and decoder style sequential architecture and trains this parameterized policy using imitation learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
1. The decomposing strategy is intuitive; however, there is not enough justification that the proposed clustering strategy is more efficient than other clustering heuristics or learning-based clustering strategies. 

2. Learning a local, improving heuristic is a widely used approach to solving routing problems. For example, NeuroLKH3 also learns a local k-opt move. The structure of the decision-making policy is similar to AM style policy. In addition, applying imitation learning to learn the structured approach is also widely used. Using GAIL as a part of imitation loss is an interesting trial; however, the effectiveness of this choice is not well validated.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
<Methodology>

1. The training method used in this study seems to be imitation learning in that it uses the difference between the recommended actions and the expert's action as a loss. I don't fully understand why the current study calls this learning agent as RL. Typically RL aims to train a sequential decision-making policy that can maximize (minimize) the future accumulated reward (loss) while assuming that the action can affect the future state transition and reward. It seems that the structured policy's role is just to match the expert action in the given context (state). If the proposed learning method is indeed RL, please describe in detail the state, action, state transition, reward, and objective.

2. How to determine the ratio between the stacked and unstacked solutions, and the size of subnodes (i.e., the size of the pie). In addition, how do these hyperparameters affect the overall solution quality and solution converging speed?


<Experiments>

1. Comparison with other decomposing strategies is necessary. Comparing the proposed method with a non-decomposing strategy is not fair. Because the current study proposes an effective decomposing strategy, it should compare with other effective decomposing strategies that can solve the large-scale CVRP.

2. It is known that imitation learning tends to overfit to the best solution. Please explain in detail how the proposed method were able to overcome these shortcomings and achieve generalization performance.
content.summary_of_the_review: Since the upper-level decomposing strategy and the lower-level TSP solver learning seem to be independent, they do not appear to be complementary. In addition, the proposed lower level solver has aspects similar to the method used in previous studies.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Thank you for the review
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the review. Please find below our responses.
- Is the proposed learning method RL? Yes, it is RL. Imitation learning is just part of the RL policy, and our overall goal is to train an RL policy to generate good solutions. We will clarify this in the appendix. 
- The ratio between the stacked and unstacked solutions: the ratio and the numbers of sub-nodes are chosen manually to achieve desirable performance.  Comparing different hyper-parameter settings is too expensive and also not very informative.
- Comparison with other decomposing strategies: L2D is a decomposition method and we have made comparisons with it.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper addresses the problem of vehicle routing problems,
esp. to learn neighborhoods for local search solvers. The authors
propose a method that combines two sub-methods: (i) to decompose
the problem into problems covered by a subset of previous  tours
(called clockwise clustering) and (ii) to learn to mimick heuristic
methods as part of an reinforcement learning approach to the
problem (called imitation improvement learning). In experiments
on 6 datasets they show that their method outperforms several
baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
s1. the problem decomposition is interesting.
s2. the combination of heuristics and reinforcement learning
  is also interesting and a very plausible approach.
s3. the authors improve the best-known-solution for some instances.

w1. the two sub-methods are not evaluated in isolation, so it
  is not clear how much each one is contributing.
w2. how the imitation improvement learning is done, is not
  fully clear. 
w3. half the experiments miss runtimes.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well written, well structured and easy to understand.
The proposed method is novel.
Reproducibility is medium (clear description, but no code).
content.summary_of_the_review:
I see three issues:
w1. the two sub-methods are not evaluated in isolation, so it
  is not clear how much each one is contributing.

  Clockwise clustering (alg. 1) could wrap any solver, not just IILSolver.
  But you did compare it only with IILSolver. By wrapping it around the
  other solvers, too, one could assess the impact of clockwise clustering
  and imitation improvement learning in isolation. Currently, we do not
  know, which of the two ideas has the major impact.

w2. how the imitation improvement learning is done, is not
  fully clear.

  In alg. 2 you call "UpdateRLWithImitation", but do not fully explain how
  that works. Are S_student and S_expert only used for the GAN-loss ?

w3. half the experiments miss runtimes. 

  For dataset 1, 3 and 4 (tab. 2 and 4) you do not report runtimes, but runtimes
  are of course crucial to asses the quality of a solver.

4. You say explicitly that for dataset 2 you used a train/test split. Did you also
  use such splits for datasets 3-6, or do you report performances of your
  model trained on the very same VRP instances?

5. The experiment from Li et al. 2021 (your table 3) originally was designed
  to show the speedup of a method, thus all methods run until they achieve
  95% of the LKH3 performance, and then you compare their runtimes.
  Could you also provide results for you method for this evaluation protocol?
  And how does HGS alone perform?
  That your runtimes are only "slightly longer" than L2D I do not see: they are
  closer to "L2D (long)", so twice the runtime of "L2D (short)".

content.title: Thank you for the review
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for reading our paper. Please find our responses below:
- Reproducibility is medium (clear description, but no code): I have already included our source code in the supplementary material.
- Clockwise clustering could wrap any solver: This is true. Our clockwise clustering can be used with other solvers. Exploring the use of  framework for other RL and heuristic algorithms would be an interesting direction for future work.
- UpdateRLWithImitation: There are some typos in the description of the GAIL. Actually, we have modified the GAIL to work with the heuristics. OUr objective was to train an Encoder network such that Encoder(student_sol) is similar to Encoder(expert_sol). Our modified GAIL should be
<$$
 \max_\theta \min_\delta  \mathbb{E}_{s\sim Expert}[ \ln (D_\delta (Encoder_\theta (s)))]  + \mathbb{E}_{s\sim Student}[ \ln (1 - D_\delta (Encoder_\theta (s)))] 
$$>
We will update the paper accordingly.
- For dataset 1, 3 and 4 (tab. 2 and 4) you do not report runtimes: The runtimes of the other heuristics are not available in the respective papers. On the other hand, for large-scale instances, heuristic methods are often run in parallel with many random seeds to avoid local optima, thus reporting running times for them does not make much sense. As such, our objective is mainly to compare solution quality. 
-  Dataset 2 you used a train/test split... : We test with train\test sets for Dataset 2 as  Li et al. (2021) already contribute such instances. For CEVRP we generate test sets in a similar way as in  Li et al. 2021. For the other datasets, since the instances are not split as train and test sets, it is difficult to verify the generalizability.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents an improvement learning-based method to generate feasible solutions for the capacitated vehicle routing problems. More specifically, an imitation learning model is trained to learn from classical heuristics to encourage the policy model to mimic and produce similar solutions. A clockwise clustering method is used to decompose a large-scale CVRP instance into subproblems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: There has been a significant amount of work of using machine learning to solve CVRP problems, as described in the paper. The motivation of this paper is to combine RL with heuristics such that RL can learn from heuristics, which I found very odd. Heuristic methods are usually very fast. Why not directly use heuristics to generate a solution? How do we expect that a ML model that learns from a heuristic performs better than the heuristic? Indeed, the experimental results are not impressive; IIL+HGS performs worse than HGS on real-world dataset 3 in Table 4. Some results in Table 3 are taken from other paper, which are not directly comparable to the results of the proposed methods, as they were generated on different machines.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Writing is clear. It seems that the source code is not available, which might make it hard to reproduce results. This paper lacks novelty, as there exist plenty of work of using ML to solve CVRP, and using imitation learning is not a significant deviation.
content.summary_of_the_review: The motivation of training a RL to mimic/learn from a heuristic using imitation learning does not make much sense. The experimental results are not significant.

content.title: Thank you for the review
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for reading our paper. Please find our responses below.

- Why not directly use heuristics to generate a solution? We believe there are only a few studies combining RL and heuristics for VRP. Especially, to the best of our knowledge, there is no RL algorithm being able to solve very-large instances, such as CVRPLIB, with competitive solutions, since heuristics are already very good in getting good solutions but are often stuck at local optima, and RL is good at escaping local optima but less scalable (only good for small-sized instances). Our framework combines RL and heuristics in a scalable and efficient way and would open new directions to solve VRP and its variants.
- Experimental results are not impressive: our algorithm is only slightly worse than the best heuristic (but better in all other datasets) in Dataset 3. This is the most challenging dataset with instances of sizes up to 30K and our algorithm still achieves competitive solutions with gaps of less than 0.04%, compared to the best heuristic. 
- Some results in Table 3 are taken from other paper ...: as explained in the paper, the computing times of the tasks in the table is extremely huge, so it is difficult to rerun all the algorithms. Our machine is clearly slower than those used to generate the other results in Table 3. In terms of solution quality, since L2D already contributes the datasets with training/testing instances, we use that to run and compare with our approach.  
- The source code is not available: We already included the source code in the supplementary material. 
- This paper lacks novelty: Our main contribution is a new framework that can handle very-large instances with competitive solutions. Previous RL algorithms are not that scalable, to the best of our knowledge.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors propose an algorithm that uses both reinforcement learning and imitation learning to seek high-quality solutions in large-scale capacitated vehicle routing problems. In summary, the algorithm works as follows. The algorithm assumes an agent’s neural network policy that applies a $k$-opt move on a given solution. Then, advanced heuristics (such as VNS and HGS) are considered as an expert for imitation learning and used to generate improved solutions upon the solutions generated by the $k$-opt learner. Finally, the solutions from advanced heuristics are learned through imitation learning together with reinforcement learning via PPO. To scale the algorithm for larger graphs, clockwise clustering (which iteratively defines angular regions and solves sub-problems in those regions in clockwise direction) is used so that the RL agent only sees the small-size problem instances and learns well on those instances. Authors evaluate their algorithm on 6 datasets and show that it works well.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
- The proposed algorithm shows good empirical performance across multiple datasets.
- The algorithm shows good scalability for larger problems.
### Weaknesses
- The algorithm is specifically designed to CVRP among various CO problems. 
- Further description for RL and IL seems required.
- The proposed idea is somewhat incremental. It is combination of RL, IL and heuristics, but nothing seems new and novel from the ML perspective.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
Some part of submission should be clarified. 
- VNS and HGS are used as *advanced* heuristics and experts for imitation learning. However, why those heuristics are powerful and how they work are not described. 
- For the $k$-opt, it seems that $k=3$ is used. However, it can be easily found that there are 7 different 3-opt moves, and it is unclear which 3-opt was used for the learning agent. 
- There are various imitation learning algorithms, e.g., one of the easiest IL algorithms we can try is behavioral cloning. However, authors used GAIL without any rationale. 
- Authors argue that clockwise clustering generates *similar* distributions for the input data. However, such similarity is ambiguous and undefined in the manuscript. 
- From the term $s(\mathcal{G}, S, \mathbb{B}, C)$, it appears that the state is different from the solution. Its definition is unclear. 
- The action space of RL is a set of $k$ nodes that corresponds to $k$-opt moves. However, the expert’s action is a bit unclear, which makes me confused about how GAIL is used. Specifically, the agent’s solution via a $k$-opt move is improved by advanced heuristics (expert), but there’s no guarantee that the improved solution can be represented by applying a $k$-opt move to the solution that was originally taken by the RL agent. Also, how to derive expert’s actions is unclear.
- In GAIL, we assume there exists a fixed expert (or data sampled from expert before training). However, the proposed algorithm seems not satisfying such condition since student solution varies and affects the expert policy’s solution space directly. In that sense, I don’t know why GAIL should be used here.
- For RL side, we need to have a well-defined reward. However, reward seems to be defined by the gap between student and expert solutions (based on Figure 2) and not dependent on the input solution to the encoder. How can we justify this? Also, the concrete definition of reward needs to be mentioned in the main part of the paper. 
- For clockwise clustering, the center point (origin) to define angular position doesn’t seem to be specified. 
- In Section 6.2., authors mentioned that HGS takes longer time and the proposed algorithm. Is this solely since HGS uses only CPU while the proposed algorithm uses GPU?
### Quality
The readability should be improved. It seems that the answers for my questions on clarity should be mentioned in the main part of the submission. 
### Novelty
The submission seems incremental and straightforward combination of RL, IL and heuristics.
### Reproducibility
Hyperparameters and results are well described and documented in the appendix.
content.summary_of_the_review: There are some items to be clarified, and the submissions seems to be a trivial combination of existing works.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1875 by Reviewer ezkU

content.title: Thank you for the review
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for reading our paper and for the detailed comments. Below we respond to your comments. We will update the paper accordingly.
- The algorithm is specifically designed to CVRP among various CO problems: We believe that CVRP is considered a difficult task in VRP, especially for larges-scale instances [1]. Recent studies also only focus on some sub-problems  of VRP such as TSP, EVRPTW, etc. 

[1] Costa, Joao Guilherme de Carvalho et al. “Learning Initialisation Heuristic for Large Scale Vehicle Routing Problem with Genetic Programming.” 2021 IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation (CEC) (2021): 1864-1871. 

- The proposed idea is somewhat incremental: We believe there are only a few studies combining RL and heuristics for VRP. Especially, to the best of our knowledge, there is no RL algorithm being able to solve very-large instances, such as CVRPLIB,  with competitive solutions, since heuristics are already very good in getting near-optimal solutions and RL is only good for small-sized instances. Our framework combines RL and heuristics in a scalable and efficient way and would open new directions to solve VRP and its variants. 
- VNS and HGS:  HGS is considered one of the best heuristic algorithms for CVRP, together with LKH-3, but HGS is more focused on CVRP and LKH-3 was designed for other variants. Our framework can be straightforwardly adapted for other heuristics.  
Besides, VNS is a popular heuristic method. The use of VNS is to see the impact of different heuristics on our IIL algorithm.  
 - k-opt: Our RL policy generates three nodes [A,B,C] and we swap in that order. RL will learn to find out which order would be good for the learning. This way allows us to generalize to 4-opt, 5-opt ,...
- Justification for GAIL: GAIL, to the best of our knowledge, is one of the best imitation learning algorithms. 
- Similar distributions for the input data: We meant instances of similar numbers of nodes.
- How GAIL works: There is a typo in the formulation of the GAIL, making it confusing. Actually, we have modified the GAIL to work with the heuristics. OUr objective was to train an Encoder network such that   Encoder(student_sol) is similar to Encoder(expert_sol). Our modified GAIL should be

<$$
 \max_\theta \min_\delta  \mathbb{E}_{s\sim Expert}[ \ln (D_\delta (Encoder_\theta (s)))]  + \mathbb{E}_{s\sim Student}[ \ln (1 - D_\delta (Encoder_\theta (s)))] 
$$>
- Rewards for RL: Such a description is missing in the current manuscript; the costs of student students are the same as the costs of the inputs.  
- Center point of the Clockwise Clustering: this is the depot.
- HGS uses only CPU ..: our IIL algorithm uses GPU for RL Policy, and CPU  for the heuristics (e.g., HGS). In other words, HGS  (done with CPU) is just part of IIL, but our proposed algorithms still run faster.
